hints: Look at the later part of the curve in Fig. 2.1 where the velocity stops increasing and becomes flat - what does that flat level tell you about the forces and the velocity?
walkthrough:
**Spot When Velocity Stops Changing**
Terminal velocity is reached when drag balances weight so there is no resultant force and velocity stays constant. On a $v$-$t$ graph that looks like the curve levelling off to become horizontal.

**Read Off the Flat Value**
In Fig. 2.1 the curve flattens from about $t = 20\text{ s}$ onwards at: $$v = 39\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is the terminal velocity.

hints: Think about what the steepness of a velocity-time graph represents at any instant, and why you need to touch the curve at only one point at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$ to find it.
Once your line is drawn, pick two widely spaced points on that straight line itself (not on the curve) and use their $v$ and $t$ values to work out its steepness.
walkthrough:
**Use Gradient for Instantaneous Acceleration**
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. On a $v$-$t$ graph: $$a = \text{gradient of } v\text{-}t \text{ graph}$$ Because the graph is curved, acceleration is changing, so you need the gradient exactly at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$. That means drawing a tangent - a straight line that just touches the curve at that point and follows its slope.

**Draw Tangent and Calculate Gradient**
Draw a good tangent at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$ extending over a large $t$-range to reduce uncertainty. Then calculate: $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ For example, using points on the tangent such as $(0, 26\text{ m s}^{-1})$ and $(18\text{ s}, 44\text{ m s}^{-1})$: $$a = \frac{44 - 26}{18 - 0} \approx 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ Any well-drawn tangent gives $0.9$ to $1.1\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Final answer: Draw tangent to curve at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$; $a =$ gradient $= \Delta v / \Delta t \approx 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$ (allow $0.9$ to $1.1\text{ m s}^{-2}$).

hints: Start by picturing the two vertical forces at time $t_1$ - which one pulls down and which one pushes up, and which is larger just after the parachute opens?
Work out the size of the downward pull due to gravity from the given mass before you combine anything.
Think about how to combine an upward force and a downward force to get the resultant force, taking care with positive and negative signs.
Recall how resultant force is linked to mass and acceleration for working out the acceleration from your resultant force.
Check the sign of your answer to decide whether the acceleration points in the same direction as the fall or opposite to it.
walkthrough:
**Identify the Two Forces**
Take downwards as positive for the calculation. Weight always acts downwards: $$W = mg$$ Drag from the parachute acts upwards, opposing motion. Just after opening, drag $= 1800\text{ N}$ is much larger than weight, so the resultant will be upwards and the skydiver will decelerate.

**Find Resultant Force**
Upward is negative if downwards is positive: $$(\Sigma)F = W - \text{drag}$$ $$(\Sigma)F = 68 \times 9.81 - 1800 \approx 667 - 1800 \approx -1133\text{ N}$$ The minus sign means the net force is about $1130\text{ N}$ upwards.

**Give Magnitude and Direction**
Magnitude is $17\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to 2 s.f. The negative sign means direction is opposite to velocity, i.e. upwards. This large upward acceleration rapidly slows the fall.

Final answer: Weight $= 68 \times 9.81 = 667\text{ N}$ downwards, drag $= 1800\text{ N}$ upwards. Resultant $F \approx -1130\text{ N}$, $a = F/m \approx -17\text{ m s}^{-2}$, so magnitude $17\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards (opposite to motion).

hints: As the skydiver slows, consider how drag and the resultant force change.
walkthrough: As speed decreases, the drag force decreases.
The resultant upward force and therefore the magnitude of the acceleration decrease, reaching zero at the new terminal speed.

hints: Think about what momentum depends on, and what the starting velocity at $t_1$ and the finishing velocity at $t_3$ are for this slowing-down interval.
Remember you can factor out the constant mass and just multiply it by the overall change in velocity, keeping the sign to show a decrease.
walkthrough:
**Use Change in Momentum**
Momentum is $p = mv$. Mass stays at $68\text{ kg}$. At $t_1$ velocity is the first terminal velocity $u = 39\text{ m s}^{-1}$ downwards. At $t_3$ velocity is $v = 5.7\text{ m s}^{-1}$ downwards. Change is final minus initial: $$\Delta p = mv - mu = m(v - u)$$

**Substitute and Calculate**
$$\Delta p = 68 \times (5.7 - 39)$$ $$\Delta p = 68 \times (-33.3) \approx -2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$$ The negative sign shows momentum decreases in the downward direction. Magnitude of change is about $2300\text{ N s}$.
Final answer: $\Delta p = m(v - u) = 68 \times (5.7 - 39) \approx -2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$, i.e. a decrease of $2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$.
